# Mitral valve prolapse

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Cardiology and angiology > Valvular heart diseases > Mitral valve prolapse*

[Original Article Link](/library/kM0mKg)

---

## Summary

<u>Mitral valve</u> prolapse (MVP) is caused by a structural defect of the <u>mitral valve</u> that results in mitral leaflets bulging into the <u>left atrium</u> during <u>systole</u>. In the US, MVP is the most common <u>heart valve</u> abnormality and the most common cause of <u>mitral regurgitation</u> (<u>MR</u>). Although MVP is typically asymptomatic, symptoms (eg., <u>palpitations</u>, fatigue, <u>dyspnea</u>) may arise, especially if associated with <u>MR</u>. A mitral prolapse click is a classic <u>auscultatory</u> finding MVP and diagnosis is made with <u>echocardiography</u>. No specific treatment is needed unless severe, symptomatic <u>MR</u> is present, in which case <u>mitral valve</u> repair or replacement is required.

---

## Epidemiology

* <u>Prevalence</u>: 2–3 % (one of the most common valvular abnormalities in the US)

* The most common cause of <u>mitral regurgitation</u> in developed countries





References:[[1]](/library/p30Ljf)[[2]](/library/h2Ycho)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

* Mostly <u>idiopathic</u>

* <u>Connective tissue disorders</u>: <u>Marfan syndrome</u>, <u>Ehlers-Danlos</u> syndrome, <u>osteogenesis imperfecta</u>

* <u>Fragile X syndrome</u> [[3]](/library/BLXz-A)

* <u>Myocardial infarction</u>: <u>infarction</u> of <u>papillary muscles</u> → rupture of chordae tendineae → <u>mitral valve</u> prolapse

* Acute <u>rheumatic heart disease</u>

* <u>Infective endocarditis</u>

* <u>Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease</u>





References:[[4]](/library/U30b3f)

---

## Pathophysiology

* The most common underlying pathology in the case of <u>mitral valve</u> prolapse is <u>myxomatous degeneration</u> (deposition of <u>glycosaminoglycan</u> such as <u>dermatan sulfate</u>) of the <u>mitral valve</u> due to a primary disease or <u>connective tissue disorder</u>

* Long, floppy <u>mitral valve</u> leaflets with excessive valvular tissue → the mitral annulus becomes dilated and the <u>chordae tendineae</u> become elongated (and may rupture) → prolapse of one or both <u>mitral valve</u> leaflets into the <u>left atrium</u> during <u>systole</u>

* The leaflets may also exhibit fibrous thickening at regions where they rub against each other.

* <u>Mitral valve</u> prolapse sets into motion a vicious cycle of events. 

* If prolapse happens without the <u>rupture of chordae tendineae</u> → <u>mitral valve</u> leaflets billow into the <u>left atrium</u> → mild to moderate <u>mitral regurgitation</u>

* If the <u>papillary muscles</u> become severely <u>ischemic</u> and the <u>chordae tendineae</u> rupture → <u>mitral valve</u> leaflets flail about in the <u>left atrium</u> → severe <u>mitral regurgitation</u>





References:[[4]](/library/U30b3f)

---

## Clinical features

* Most patients are asymptomatic.

* Rarely: atypical <u>chest pain</u> and <u>anxiety</u>

* In case of complications: fatigue, <u>dyspnea</u>, <u>cough</u>, <u>syncope</u>, and <u>palpitations</u> (see “Complications” below)

* <u>Auscultatory</u> findings 

* Mitral valve prolapse click: high-frequency, midsystolic click that is best heard at the <u>mitral region</u>

* High-frequency, mid-to-late systolic <u>murmur</u> that is best heard at the <u>mitral region</u> and may radiate to the <u>axilla</u> (squatting diminishes the <u>murmur</u>)

* Patients with severe <u>MR</u>: <u>S3</u> may be heard as a result of <u>left ventricular</u> overload (especially in the left <u>decubitus position</u>)

## Diagnosis

* <u>ECG</u>: mostly normal

* <u>Transthoracic echocardiography</u> (test of choice) to confirm diagnosis
* <u>Echocardiographic</u> definition of MVP: displacement of the <u>mitral valve</u> during <u>systole</u> by more than 2 mm above the <u>mitral valve</u> annulus in the parasternal long-axis view

* Classical MVP (∼ 60%): leaflet thickness â¥ 5 mm

* Non-classical MVP (∼ 40%): leaflet thickness < 5 mm

* <u>Transesophageal echocardiography</u> (<u>TEE</u>) is used as an adjunct to <u>TTE</u> and intraoperatively to guide <u>mitral valve</u> repair procedures.





References:[[4]](/library/U30b3f)

---

## Treatment

* No treatment is required in most cases.

* Patients with severe <u>mitral regurgitation</u> : <u>mitral valve</u> repair or replacement (see “Therapy” in “<u>Mitral regurgitation</u>”)

* Additional treatment is required when complications arise (see “Complications” below)





References:[[4]](/library/U30b3f)

---

## Complications

* <u>Atrial fibrillation</u>

* Ventricular ectopics : MVP patients with ventricular ectopics should be asked to avoid <u>caffeine</u>; <u>β-blockers</u> may be used for symptomatic relief.

* <u>Transient ischemic attacks</u> (<u>TIA</u>) and/or <u>stroke</u> : Patients who experience <u>TIA</u> or <u>stroke</u> will require prophylactic doses of <u>aspirin</u> (also see “Therapy” in <u>stroke</u>)

* <u>Infective endocarditis</u> : MVP patients with a past history of <u>infective endocarditis</u> require prophylaxis against <u>infective endocarditis</u> (see <u>prophylaxis for endocarditis</u>).

* <u>Right heart failure</u>

* <u>Sudden cardiac death</u> (rare)





References:[[5]](/library/6ZYjcn)[[6]](/library/pZYLcn)[[7]](/library/R2Ylho)




We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.
